meta.title: Maternal health and doulas, 18 days of posts
meta.subject: maternal health policy in Texas — maternal mortality and morbidity, Medicaid postpartum coverage and doula reimbursement, the definition and certification of doulas, HHSC and DSHS maternal programs, the maternal mortality review committee, and county maternal-health funding in Houston, Austin and San Antonio
meta.subtitle: Oct 1 to Oct 18, 2026. Each dot is one post with 1K+ views about Texas maternal health and doula policy, plus every post repeating an earlier one, in the lane for what it argues. Higher and bigger means more views. White means 90% or more the same words as an earlier post, with a white line back to it. Coloured lines link a post to the post it quoted or replied to. Updated daily.

lanes.label: Abortion ban is killing mothers
lanes.description: Texas's abortion ban (SB 8, post-Dobbs near-total ban) is causally driving higher maternal deaths, citing rising mortality figures and comparisons with ban versus non-ban states.

lanes.label: Mortality report delay is cover-up
lanes.description: The state is delaying or withholding the maternal mortality review committee report and 2022-2023 data for political reasons, such as the midterms, to hide the ban's harms.

lanes.label: Black maternal health disparity crisis
lanes.description: Black women in Texas, especially in Harris County, face far higher maternal death rates, and candidates and advocates must fix this racial disparity.

lanes.label: Ban-blame claims are misleading
lanes.description: Claims linking Texas's abortion laws to rising maternal mortality are misleading or false, with statistics misread and politicians accused of lying.

lanes.label: Medicaid, doulas and funding solutions
lanes.description: Texas should expand postpartum Medicaid, reimburse and certify doulas, and fund county and rural maternal-health programs to improve outcomes.

lanes.label: Pushback
lanes.description: Posts doubting, mocking, fact-checking or arguing against the dominant framings.

posts.name: J_Grant_C
posts.text:
@LunaForTruth How many deaths versus births have happened since the abortion ban in Texas

Texas’s early-pregnancy abortion ban (SB 8) took effect September 1, 2021, and a near-total ban followed after Dobbs in 2022. Research comparing observed outcomes with expected trends finds thousands of additional births and a much smaller rise in infant and maternal deaths.

Births
A Johns Hopkins study in JAMA estimated that SB 8 was associated with 9,799 additional births in Texas from April through December 2022 (297,088 observed vs. 287,289 expected under a synthetic-control counterfactual)—about a 3% increase. The pattern was not seen in other states. A University of Houston analysis of CDC data reported more than 16,000 more births in 2022 than in 2021 (about a 2% rise in the fertility rate), with larger increases among Hispanic women. Broader work on states with bans estimated roughly 22,000 more births than expected across those states, with Texas accounting for a large share. Later access to out-of-state care and mailed medication abortion has reduced the share of pregnancies carried to term that would otherwise have been aborted.

Infant deaths
Infant deaths in Texas rose from 1,985 in 2021 to 2,240 in 2022 (+255, or 12.9%), versus a 1.8% rise in the rest of the U.S. A JAMA Pediatrics counterfactual analysis estimated about 216 excess infant deaths from March to December 2022 (12.7% above expectation; confidence interval wide and including zero at the low end). The increase was concentrated in congenital anomalies (up about 23% in Texas while falling slightly elsewhere)—conditions often diagnosed after six weeks and previously a common reason for abortion. A later multi-state analysis attributed most of an estimated 478 excess infant deaths in ban states to Texas (about 384).

Maternal deaths
These numbers are far smaller. ProPublica’s analysis of Texas hospital data found 79 in-hospital deaths of pregnant or postpartum women in 2018–2019 versus 120 in 2022–2023. CDC-based analyses report the Texas maternal mortality rate up about 33% from 2019 to 2023 while the national rate fell about 7.5%; one analysis put the 2022 rate increase at 56%. Sepsis among women hospitalized for second-trimester pregnancy loss rose more than 50% after the ban. Absolute maternal deaths remain on the order of dozens per year in a state with roughly 370,000–400,000 births annually.

Scale
In the first post-ban birth window that has been studied carefully, additional births were on the order of ~10,000, excess infant deaths in the low hundreds, and excess maternal deaths in the tens. Studies treat the ban as associated with these shifts after accounting for other states’ trends, but they do not claim every extra birth or death is caused only by the law; COVID-era disruptions, care access, and continued out-of-state or medication abortions all affect the totals.
